🚀 Hook: Why Most RAG Systems Fail Before Retrieval Even Starts

Most engineers think RAG quality depends mainly on:

The LLM

The vector database

The embeddings

But in reality? Many RAG systems fail long before retrieval happens. Why? Because the data entering the pipeline is:

Messy

Duplicated

Noisy

Unstructured

Poorly selected

And here’s the dangerous part:

Garbage in → hallucinations out. Even the best retrieval pipeline cannot save low-quality ingestion. This is why ingestion is one of the most important — and most ignored — parts of production RAG systems. 🧠 Basic Intuition: What is Ingestion? At a high level:

Ingestion is the process of preparing raw data for AI retrieval systems. Think of it like preparing ingredients before cooking. You don’t throw:

Plastic wrappers

Rotten vegetables

Entire boxes

into a recipe. You:

Clean

Cut

Organize

Prepare

RAG ingestion works the same way. 📦 What Counts as “Documents” in RAG?

RAG: Retrieval Augmented Generation — The Complete Guide

Janvinaikwork

8 min read

·

Just now

--

From zero to interview ready, everything in one place. No prerequisites. What is RAG? RAG stands for

Retrieval Augmented Generation

. It is not a new model or a completely new technology. It is a technique used to make Large Language Models smarter by giving them access to external data while generating answers. A standard LLM like GPT or Gemini is trained on data available up to a certain point in time. After that, it does not automatically learn anything new. It also has no awareness of private information such as company documents, internal databases, product manuals, or FAQs. RAG solves this problem. In simple terms, RAG works in three steps:

Retrieve relevant information from a knowledge base

Provide that information to the LLM

Generate an answer using the retrieved context

A good real world example is

NotebookLM by Google

. You upload a PDF, ask questions, and it responds while pointing to the exact paragraph it used.

real world example is NotebookLM by Google . You upload a PDF, ask questions, and it responds while pointing to the exact paragraph it used. The model does not memorise your document. Instead, it retrieves the relevant information first and then generates the response. That is RAG in practice. The Problem RAG Solves

A standard LLM behaves like a student preparing for a

closed book exam

. It can only answer based on what it memorised during training. If you ask something outside that knowledge, it may either say “I don’t know” or confidently generate an incorrect answer. This behaviour is known as

hallucination

. Imagine building a customer support chatbot for a fintech company. Users may ask:

“What is the current interest rate on my savings account?”

“Was there a policy update last week?”

The information required to answer these questions is private and changes frequently. Without RAG, you are left with two poor options:

Do nothing

— The LLM hallucinates or says it does not know. Users lose trust. Retrain the model

— Expensive, time consuming, and must be repeated whenever data changes. Neither solution is practical.

it does not know. Users lose trust. Retrain the model — Expensive, time consuming, and must be repeated whenever data changes. Neither solution is practical. RAG fills this gap by allowing the model to access updated and private information

during inference

. Three Ways to Give LLMs Knowledge

Before understanding RAG deeply, it helps to compare it with the other common approaches. Fine Tuning

retrains the model on custom data. It gives fast inference and specialised behaviour, but it is expensive, difficult to update, and can still hallucinate. Prompt Stuffing

places large amounts of information directly into the prompt. It is simple to get started with, but is limited by the context window and becomes costly at scale. RAG

retrieves relevant chunks during query time. It is cheap, scalable, and easy to update — though slightly slower and dependent on retrieval quality. Think about it like this:

Fine tuning is like sending an employee for six months of training so they memorise the handbook. Prompt stuffing is like handing them a 500 page handbook five minutes before a meeting. RAG is like giving them access to a

well organised filing cabinet

where they can instantly find the exact information they need.

before a meeting. RAG is like giving them access to a well organised filing cabinet where they can instantly find the exact information they need. Key Benefits of RAG

1. Reduces Hallucinations

LLMs hallucinate when they attempt to answer without reliable information. RAG grounds the response in retrieved documents, making answers more accurate and trustworthy. 2. Keeps Knowledge Up to Date

Every LLM has a knowledge cutoff date. With RAG, the knowledge base is separate from the model itself. Updating the database automatically updates what the model can access. 3. Cost Effective

Fine tuning can cost thousands of dollars and require weeks of compute time. RAG is comparatively inexpensive because you only maintain and query a document database. 4. Better Data Privacy

With fine tuning, private data becomes part of the model weights. With RAG, the data stays inside your own systems and only the relevant chunks are shared during query time. This is especially important in healthcare, finance, and legal domains. The RAG Pipeline

RAG systems operate in two phases:

Ingestion Pipeline

— runs once or whenever data changes; processes and stores documents

Retrieval Pipeline

— runs for every user query; retrieves relevant chunks and generates responses

A.

runs once or whenever data changes; processes and stores documents Retrieval Pipeline — runs for every user query; retrieves relevant chunks and generates responses A. Ingestion Pipeline (Data Preparation)

Step 1: Data Extraction

The first step is collecting raw data from different sources such as PDFs, websites, Word documents, Excel sheets, databases, Notion pages, and Slack conversations. Frameworks like LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Haystack provide built-in document loaders for many of these formats. Step 2: Chunking

After extracting the text, the content is split into smaller sections called

chunks

. Chunking is necessary because LLMs have context window limits. Passing an entire 200 page document into a prompt would be expensive, inefficient, and often impossible. More importantly, users usually need only a small portion of the document. If someone asks about a refund policy, you only need the relevant paragraphs rather than the entire handbook. Poor chunking strategies can significantly reduce RAG quality. Chunks that cut sentences in half, mix unrelated topics, or lose context produce weak retrieval results. Here are the common chunking strategies:

Size-based chunking with overlap

— Splits text after a fixed number of tokens while sharing overlapping content. Reliable production default. Sentence-based chunking

— Splits content using sentence boundaries.

overlap — Splits text after a fixed number of tokens while sharing overlapping content. Reliable production default. Sentence-based chunking — Splits content using sentence boundaries. Best for general text documents. Structure-based chunking

— Splits by headings, sections, or paragraphs. Best for reports and structured documentation. Semantic chunking

— Splits based on topic changes detected using embeddings. Higher quality retrieval but slower. In production systems,

size-based chunking with overlap

is the most commonly used strategy because it works consistently across different document types. Step 3: Embeddings

Computers cannot directly understand meaning in language — they work with numbers. Each chunk is converted into a

vector embedding

, which is a numerical representation of semantic meaning. For example, the text

“The refund policy allows 30 day returns”

becomes a vector like

[0.23, -0.45, 0.67, 0.12, -0.89, ...]

. Texts with similar meanings generate vectors that are close to each other mathematically. This enables

semantic similarity search

. Some popular embedding models:

sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2

— 384 dimensions, free

OpenAI text-embedding-3-small

— 1536 dimensions, paid

Google Gemini Embeddings

— 768 dimensions, paid

Step 4: Storing in a Vector Database

The chunk text and its embedding are stored in a

vector database

designed specifically for similarity search.

paid Step 4: Storing in a Vector Database The chunk text and its embedding are stored in a vector database designed specifically for similarity search. Similarity between vectors is commonly measured using

cosine similarity

:

cos(θ) = (A · B) / (|A| × |B|)

The closer the angle is to zero, the more semantically similar the two vectors are. Popular vector databases:

FAISS

— Open source and local projects

ChromaDB

— Lightweight and beginner friendly

Pinecone

— Managed cloud deployments

Elasticsearch

— Combines keyword and vector search

A note on Hybrid Search

Semantic search is excellent for understanding meaning, but it may fail with exact identifiers such as order IDs, invoice numbers, or product codes. Keyword search methods like BM25 are better for exact matches. Combining both approaches is called

hybrid search

, and it consistently performs better in production systems. B.

methods like BM25 are better for exact matches. Combining both approaches is called hybrid search , and it consistently performs better in production systems. B. Retrieval Pipeline (Query Processing)

When a user asks a question, the system:

Converts the query into an embedding

using the same embedding model used during ingestion

Fetches the top K most relevant chunks

from the vector database

Augments the prompt

by adding the retrieved chunks as context

Generates a grounded response

using the LLM

One critical rule: the

same embedding model must be used during both ingestion and retrieval

. Different embedding models generate vectors in different numerical spaces. If the models do not match, similarity comparisons become meaningless and retrieval quality breaks completely. Here is what an augmented prompt looks like in practice:

System:

You are a helpful assistant. Answer using only the provided context. Context:

Chunk 1: Electronics can be returned within 15 days of purchase. Chunk 2: Items must be returned in their original packaging with all accessories. Question:

What is the return policy for electronics? Advanced RAG Architectures

As RAG systems mature, several specialised architectures have emerged:

Naive RAG

— Basic retrieve-and-generate flow. Best for simple question answering. Hybrid RAG

— Combines semantic and keyword search.

mature, several specialised architectures have emerged: Naive RAG — Basic retrieve-and-generate flow. Best for simple question answering. Hybrid RAG — Combines semantic and keyword search. Best for product codes, IDs, and exact terms. RAG with Memory

— Maintains conversational context. Best for multi-turn chatbots. Graph RAG

— Uses graph relationships between entities. Best for legal, compliance, and fraud analysis. Agentic RAG

— Agent decides whether to search, call APIs, or reason further. Best for complex multi-step tasks. Multimodal RAG

— Handles text, images, audio, and video. Best for multimedia knowledge bases. Self RAG

— Model critiques and improves its own response. Best for high accuracy applications. Interview Questions

Q1. What is RAG and why was it introduced? RAG is a technique that connects an LLM to an external knowledge base during query time. It was introduced to solve hallucinations, knowledge cutoff limitations, and lack of access to private data — without requiring expensive retraining. Q2. Do we still need the raw document after it has been vectorised? Yes. The embedding vector is only used to locate relevant chunks. The LLM still requires the original text to generate responses. Q3. What is a vector embedding and why do we convert text into numbers?

chunks. The LLM still requires the original text to generate responses. Q3. What is a vector embedding and why do we convert text into numbers? A vector embedding is a numerical representation of semantic meaning. Computers cannot compare language directly, but they can compare numerical vectors. Similar texts generate similar vectors, enabling semantic retrieval. Q4. What is cosine similarity and why is it used in RAG? Cosine similarity measures how similar two vectors are by comparing the angle between them. If the vectors point in similar directions, the texts are semantically related. This is why cosine similarity is commonly used in vector search systems. Q5. Why do we chunk documents instead of passing the entire document to the LLM? LLMs have context window limitations. Large documents may not fit into the prompt, and including unnecessary information increases both cost and response noise. Chunking helps retrieve only the most relevant information. Q6. Which chunking strategy is commonly used in production? Size-based chunking with overlap is the most common production choice because it is simple, reliable, and effective across many document types. Overlap also prevents loss of context between chunks. Q7. What is the difference between semantic search and lexical search?

and effective across many document types. Overlap also prevents loss of context between chunks. Q7. What is the difference between semantic search and lexical search? Semantic search retrieves conceptually related content using embeddings. Lexical search focuses on exact keyword matching. Semantic search may miss exact identifiers, while lexical search may fail to understand paraphrased meaning. Hybrid search combines the strengths of both. Q8. Why must the same embedding model be used during ingestion and retrieval? Each embedding model creates vectors in its own numerical space. Similarity calculations only work correctly when both stored chunks and queries are generated using the same model. Q9. What is the difference between Fine Tuning, Prompt Stuffing, and RAG? Fine Tuning

stores knowledge inside model weights. Expensive and difficult to update. Prompt Stuffing

adds knowledge directly into prompts. Low cost but limited by the context window. RAG

retrieves knowledge during query time. Low cost and easily updated. Q10. What is Agentic RAG and how is it different from standard RAG? Standard RAG performs one retrieval step followed by generation. Agentic RAG adds reasoning and decision making.

RAG and how is it different from standard RAG? Standard RAG performs one retrieval step followed by generation. Agentic RAG adds reasoning and decision making. The agent can decide whether to search a database, call an API, search the web, or break the query into smaller tasks — before generating the final response. It is useful for complex workflows where a single retrieval step is not enough.

Why neither is enough on its own

Part of the series:

How Search Understands Meaning

In the

last post

, we used this mental model:

similarity search = engine

semantic search = full car

But that raises another question:

What powers the car itself? Because semantic systems don’t rely on a single retrieval method. They usually combine:

vector search (meaning)

keyword search (exact matching)

And both solve different problems. What

Modern search systems generally use two approaches:

Keyword search

→ exact term matching

Vector search

→ semantic similarity

Most production systems use both. Because each one fails differently. Why

Users don’t always search using exact words. Example:

“affordable notebook”

A user probably means:

“cheap laptop”

Keyword search may miss that entirely. But vector search can understand the semantic similarity. Now reverse it. Query:

“iPhone 13 Pro”

Here, exact words matter. And keyword search often performs better than vectors. That’s the core tradeoff. Now, how it actually works 👇

Traditional search engines use approaches like BM25. The idea is simple:

match exact terms

score documents based on relevance

rank results accordingly

Keyword search cares about:

which words appear

how often they appear

how rare they are across documents

(Inverse Document Frequency / IDF)

Rare terms like: “PostgreSQL” carry more ranking weight than common words like: “database”

2. What keyword search is good at

Keyword search is excellent for:

exact names

product IDs

error codes

technical terms

precise queries

Example:

Query:

“iPhone 13 Pro”

Keyword search understands:

exact words matter

exact ordering matters

That gives it very high precision. 3. Where keyword search fails

It does not understand meaning. Example:

Query:

“affordable notebook”

Document:

“cheap laptop for students”

The meaning matches. The words don’t. So keyword systems may rank it poorly or miss it entirely. 4. Vector search (semantic retrieval)

Vector search works differently. Instead of matching exact words:

Now the system can compare:

meaning

intent

semantic similarity

instead of exact keywords. At scale, systems usually use Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexes like HNSW or FAISS to make similarity search fast enough for millions of vectors. 5. What vector search is good at

Vector search is strong when:

wording changes

queries are conversational

users describe intent naturally

Example:

“how to fix wifi”

can match:

“troubleshooting internet connectivity”

Even though almost none of the keywords overlap. That’s the power of semantic similarity. 6. Where vector search fails

Vector search can lose precision. Example:

Query:

“iPhone 13 Pro”

Vector search might retrieve:

iPhone 14

Apple accessories

other premium phones

Because semantically:

they are related

But the user wanted:

exact match

This is where keyword search wins. 7.

iPhone 14 Apple accessories other premium phones Because semantically: they are related But the user wanted: exact match This is where keyword search wins. 7. Side-by-side comparison

| Problem | Keyword Search | Vector Search |

|---|---|---|

| Exact match | ✅ Strong | ❌ Weaker |

| Synonyms | ❌ Weak | ✅ Strong |

| Semantic understanding | ⚠️ Limited | ✅ Strong |

| Precision | ✅ High | ⚠️ Variable |

| Conversational queries | ❌ Weak | ✅ Strong |

8. The real insight

These systems fail in opposite ways. Keyword search:

understands exact words

misses meaning

Vector search:

understands meaning

misses exact precision

That’s why modern retrieval systems rarely rely on only one. 9. Mental model

Think of it like this:

keyword search = literal matching

vector search = meaning matching

One matches what you said. The other matches what you meant. Final takeaway

Keyword search and vector search solve different problems. And the key idea:

Precision and meaning are separate signals. Modern systems combine both. What’s next

In the next post, we’ll combine these ideas:

Hybrid search: combining sparse and dense signals into one retrieval system. That’s where modern search systems start to get really powerful.
